prompt: Explain the pros and cons of personality tests as a selection tool, using the criteria for selection methods. Would you ultimately recommend them?
modelAnswer: Validity: some traits predict performance in specific jobs (conscientiousness broadly; emotional stability for supervisors, persistence for sales), and the case cites predictive power similar to interviews – but only if the trait is linked to the job analysis; generic tests have modest validity and faking lowers it. Reliability: standardised, scored the same way for everyone – high consistency across raters; but applicants inflate positive traits when applying, so results differ from honest answers. Practicability: cheap, fast, scalable for many applicants, online; but candidates may find intrusive items unacceptable, and there are legal/privacy and bias concerns (cultural norms, disability). Recommendation: not as a stand-alone or knock-out tool; use only validated, job-related tests, combined with structured interviews and work samples, interpret results in a follow-up conversation, and consider practicability (cost per hire, volume). Faking can be reduced with forced-choice formats and consistency checks.
keyPoints: Validity: job-related traits vs generic tests, faking
Practicability: cheap, scalable; acceptance, legal issues
Conditional recommendation, combined with other methods

prompt: Which selection methods would you recommend instead of personality tests to ensure person–organisation fit?
modelAnswer: First define the organisation's values and the job requirements (job analysis) and set criteria in advance – fit must mean shared values and goals, not “people like us” (similar-to-me bias). Methods: structured behavioural and situational interviews with questions on values in action (“tell me about a time…”) and scoring guides – valid and reliable; work samples, role-plays or an assessment centre showing how candidates behave in realistic situations (teamwork, customer contact); realistic job previews (informing, not only attracting) so candidates can self-select – fit works both ways; trial days or meeting future colleagues; references focused on behaviour. Use diverse, trained panels to reduce bias, and combine methods so each criterion is covered without unnecessary repetition (cost-effectiveness).
keyPoints: Define P–O fit via values, not similarity

prompt: Referring to concepts taught in class, explain three reasons why a piece rate may not be ideal as an incentive plan for Safelite's installers.
modelAnswer: 1) Control and contingency: output depends on others – scheduling, routing, warehouse picking, wrong or damaged glass – and on weather-driven demand; the installer cannot fully control the measured result, so expectancy (effort → performance) is weakened and pay feels unfair. 2) Measurement matches only part of the goal: units installed ignore quality, safety and customer service; piece rates invite rushing, defects and leaks (unless rework is unpaid); cooperation with warehouse and colleagues is not rewarded. 3) Pay uncertainty: income fluctuates with demand (storms vs quiet weeks) – insecurity, stress, overwork; agency theory: risk-averse employees want a premium for bearing risk. Also: interdependent work where individual incentives undermine collaboration, and potential crowding-out of intrinsic motivation.

prompt: As Head of HR, which incentive plan would you introduce instead of a pure piece rate, and why?
modelAnswer: A mixed plan: a guaranteed base wage (security, reduces pay uncertainty) plus variable pay. Variable part: (a) individual piece-rate bonus above a threshold, with a quality condition – unpaid rework of defects and customer-satisfaction scores; (b) a team or branch component (installers + warehouse + scheduling) tied to jobs completed, quality and on-time rate, to reward the interdependent process and encourage cooperation (collective PFP: alignment vs line of sight). Make it clear, smooth and secure: rules and KPIs set and discussed in advance, frequent feedback, measurement over longer periods or across a team to smooth weather-driven swings, higher share of base pay. Contingency and contiguity: pay quickly after performance. Check the conditions for PRP: measure matches goal (units + quality), employee controls much of the result, results known before payment – then PRP works, as Lazear found productivity rising when piece rates were combined with a guaranteed minimum.
keyPoints: Justified with PRP conditions / Lazear evidence
